repos.name: JustVugg / colibri
repos.description: Run frontier MoE models on hardware you already own — pure C, zero deps, experts streamed from disk. Tiny engine, immense model. 🐦

summary.goal: Colibrì is a pure-C inference engine designed to run frontier Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models ranging from 744B to 2.8T parameters on consumer and heterogeneous hardware. It treats storage, RAM, and VRAM as a single inference memory hierarchy, and is described as both a usable engine and an open research platform for inference-side performance work.
summary.usage: Users can download a prebuilt release or build from source with `git clone https://github.com/JustVugg/colibri && cd colibri/c` followed by `./setup.sh`. After obtaining a converted model (e.g., a ~372GB GLM-5.2 container from Hugging Face), the engine is run with commands such as `./coli chat`, `./coli serve`, or `./coli web`.
summary.pros: Nine model families (including GLM-5.2, Kimi K3, and OLMoE) share the same `coli chat`/`coli serve`/`coli web` front end, and none of the supported models requires a GPU. A learning cache records routing history so the engine becomes faster the more it is used, and an optional dual-SSD setup can increase aggregate read bandwidth for streaming experts.
summary.cons: Model weights are large -- the reference GLM-5.2 container is about 372GB, and other families range up to roughly 1.6TB for Kimi K3, so a sizeable, ideally fast, disk appears to be a prerequisite. The README also states there is no SLA on inference speed, only a guarantee on model semantics, so performance may vary with available fast memory and drive characteristics such as O_DIRECT support.
summary.fit: This project appears best suited to users who already own consumer or heterogeneous hardware (CPU, optional GPU, and adequate disk) and want to run very large MoE models locally rather than through a hosted API. It may also suit those interested in contributing to or experimenting with inference-systems research, given its stated role as an open research platform.

repos.name: alibaba / open-code-review
repos.description: Fast, efficient, battle-tested at Alibaba's scale. Hybrid architecture code review tool: deterministic pipelines + LLM Agent, precise line-level comments, built-in multi-language ruleset (NPE, thread-safety, XSS, SQL injection), OpenAI & Anthropic compatible.

summary.goal: Open Code Review (ocr) is an AI-powered code review command-line tool originally built internally at Alibaba Group and later open-sourced; it reads Git diffs and sends changed files to a configurable LLM via an agent to generate structured, line-level review comments, with an additional `ocr scan` command for reviewing entire files or directories without a diff.
summary.usage: Install globally with `npm install -g @alibaba-group/open-code-review`, then run `ocr config provider` and `ocr config model` to set up an LLM (unless using Delegation Mode). Reviews are run with commands such as `ocr review` for workspace or branch-range changes, `ocr review --commit <id>` for a single commit, and `ocr scan` for full-file audits of a repository or directory.
summary.pros: The design combines deterministic engineering (precise file selection, smart file bundling, rule matching, positioning/reflection modules) with an agent for dynamic decisions, aiming for more stable and predictable review quality than general-purpose agents. On the documented AACR-Bench benchmark (50 repos, 200 PRs, 10 languages, 1,505 annotated issues), it reports higher Precision and F1 than Claude Code using the same model, while consuming roughly 1/9 of the tokens and completing reviews faster.
summary.cons: The same AACR-Bench results show lower Recall than general-purpose agents; this is documented as a deliberate trade-off favoring precision over noise, meaning some real defects may go unreported compared to broader-coverage tools.
summary.fit: Based on the documented CLI commands, benchmark comparisons, and integrations, the tool appears best suited for teams wanting automated, git-native code review in CI/CD pipelines or alongside coding agents such as Claude Code, Codex, and Cursor, though this fit is inferred from the documented features and integrations rather than explicitly stated.

repos.name: multimodal-art-projection / YuE
repos.description: YuE2: frontier music generation with symbolic planning, zero-shot covers, and agentic music editing.

summary.goal: YuE2 is a music generation project aiming to unify symbolic (score-based) and audio music generation. Given lyrics and a style prompt, it produces an editable melody-and-chord plan, then renders that plan into a complete song with vocals and accompaniment.
summary.usage: After cloning the repository, users create a Python 3.12 virtual environment, run `python -m pip install .`, and execute `python examples/generate.py --output outputs/first-song`. A staged Python API (plan → generate_semantic → synthesize → decode) using `YuE2Pipeline.from_pretrained("m-a-p/YuE2-3B")` is also documented, and model files download from Hugging Face on first use.
summary.pros: The README reports YuE2 (best-of-8) achieving a 6.9632 SongBench Avg on WildSongBench, described as the highest observed mean among evaluated settings, and states it is competitive with Suno v5/v6. It also highlights an editable symbolic score as a white-box interface for inspecting and revising a composition before audio rendering.
summary.cons: Quick start requires a Linux system with an NVIDIA GPU supporting BF16 and 24 GB VRAM, which likely limits usability on lower-end or non-Linux hardware. Editing a composition also generates an entirely new recording rather than preserving the original waveform outside the edited section.
summary.fit: This project appears suited for users or agents wanting controllable, score-based song generation, zero-shot covers, and iterative musical editing via an agent skill, rather than simple one-shot audio generation without inspectable intermediate structure.

repos.name: debpalash / VoiceStudio
repos.description: VoiceStudio is the open-source, fully-local ElevenLabs alternative — voice cloning, voice design, video dubbing, dictation, transcription & audiobook creation in 646 languages.

summary.goal: VoiceStudio is a locally-run application for voice cloning, video dubbing, dictation, and long-form audio production, using 16 TTS engines, 11 ASR engines, and a catalogue spanning 646 languages, with no account or subscription required for the local workflow.
summary.usage: Users install VoiceStudio by downloading a package from the latest GitHub release, or run it via Docker with `docker run -d -p 127.0.0.1:3900:3900 -v omnivoice-data:/app/omnivoice_data --name voicestudio palashdeb/omnivoice-studio:stable`. Running from source needs Node 20+/Bun and Python 3.11+, then `git clone https://github.com/debpalash/VoiceStudio.git`, `bun install`, and `bun run desktop`.
summary.pros: VoiceStudio keeps voices, projects, and outputs on the local machine by default, describes its source, engines, models, API, and routing as open, and provides an OpenAI-compatible API and an MCP server for integrations.
summary.cons: VoiceStudio's main branch is described as active beta software that may change between releases, and Intel Macs cannot run its local Python backend, requiring a remote backend instead.
summary.fit: VoiceStudio appears best suited for private, offline, self-hosted, or high-volume use where the user supplies the hardware, licensed under AGPL-3.0, in contrast to hosted voice services that manage compute via subscription.

repos.name: 666ghj / MiroFish
repos.description: A Simple and Universal Swarm Intelligence Engine, Predicting Anything. 简洁通用的群体智能引擎，预测万物

summary.goal: MiroFish is presented as a next-generation, multi-agent AI prediction engine. It reportedly extracts seed information from real-world sources (such as news, policy drafts, or financial signals) and builds a simulated digital world where many independent agents interact, allowing users to inject variables and observe projected outcomes.
summary.usage: Source deployment requires Node.js 18+, Python between 3.11 and 3.12, and the uv package manager. Setup involves copying `.env.example` to `.env` with API keys, then running `npm run setup:all` to install dependencies and `npm run dev` to start the frontend (http://localhost:3000) and backend (http://localhost:5001). A Docker option is also available via `docker compose up -d`.
summary.pros: The documented workflow spans graph building, environment setup, simulation, report generation, and deep interaction with simulated agents. It supports any LLM API using the OpenAI SDK format, and its simulation engine is built on the open-source OASIS project from the CAMEL-AI team.
summary.cons: Setup requires configuring both an LLM API key and a Zep Cloud API key before use. The README also notes that simulations can be resource-intensive, recommending users first try runs of fewer than 40 rounds due to high consumption.
summary.fit: Based on its stated vision, MiroFish may suit decision-makers wanting to rehearse policies or public relations scenarios, as well as individual users exploring creative or speculative simulations, though the README does not specify infrastructure needs for larger-scale deployments.

repos.name: Panniantong / Agent-Reach
repos.description: Give your AI agent eyes to see the entire internet. Read & search Twitter, Reddit, YouTube, GitHub, Bilibili, XiaoHongShu — one CLI, zero API fees.

summary.goal: Agent Reach is documented as a capability layer that equips shell-capable AI agents (e.g., Claude Code, OpenClaw, Cursor, Windsurf) with internet access — reading web pages, YouTube subtitles, GitHub repositories, Twitter/X, Reddit, Bilibili, RSS, and more — by selecting, installing, and health-checking the most stable integration method for each platform.
summary.usage: To install, the README instructs copying the message '帮我安装 Agent Reach：https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Panniantong/agent-reach/main/docs/install.md' to a shell-capable AI agent, which runs the setup. Installation status can be checked with `agent-reach doctor`, and the tool can be removed with `agent-reach uninstall`.
summary.pros: All tools and APIs are described as free and open source, with credentials stored only locally rather than uploaded. Each platform reportedly uses a prioritized list of primary and backup backends, so if one integration breaks the tool can switch to another without user intervention, and `agent-reach doctor` reports each channel's current backend status.
summary.cons: Several platforms — including Reddit, Facebook, Instagram, and Xiaohongshu — reportedly have no zero-configuration path and require login via a desktop OpenCLI browser session or manually exported cookies. The README also cautions that cookie-based logins on platforms like Twitter and Xiaohongshu carry a risk of account suspension, recommending dedicated secondary accounts rather than primary ones.
summary.fit: This appears suited for users operating a shell-capable AI agent (e.g., Claude Code, OpenClaw, Cursor) who want to add internet-reading and search abilities without manually configuring each platform's API. It requires Python 3.10+, and server deployments reportedly need a proxy costing about $1/month, while local use reportedly does not.

repos.name: asgeirtj / system_prompts_leaks

summary.pros: Coverage spans many providers and products, including chat, coding-agent, and API variants, with a frequently updated 'Most recent additions/changes' table (lines 34-58); the project has reportedly been referenced by outside publications such as The Washington Post and CEPS' AI World (lines 20, 22).
summary.cons: Because entries are described as leaked prompts, the README does not document an independent verification process confirming each file's authenticity or that a given prompt remains current for its product (inference).
summary.fit: This resource appears suited to researchers, prompt engineers, and AI practitioners studying system prompt structure and conventions across products, rather than to those seeking an installable tool or software library (inference).

repos.name: rlaope / oh-my-hermes
repos.description: All in one plugin for Hermes Agent ⚚ the coding intelligence, a long-term memory system and model optimized workflow packages

summary.goal: oh-my-hermes (OMH) is described as an operating layer installed on top of Hermes Agent (NousResearch) that adds planning, research, coding handoffs, operations, and project memory with explicit evidence boundaries, aiming to turn a Hermes Agent request into a clear capability, a concrete next step, and an honest record of what happened.
summary.usage: Installation uses a shell script (curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rlaope/oh-my-hermes/main/install.sh | sh) on macOS/Linux or a PowerShell command (irm https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rlaope/oh-my-hermes/main/install.ps1 | iex) on Windows, followed by the required omh setup step; omh update refreshes the installed command, managed skills, and Hermes registration afterward.
summary.pros: Documented capabilities include mixture-of-models routing across nine editable categories, a catalog of 108 omh-* specialist skills, nine ulw- workflow engines, a file-backed long-term memory system kept separate from Hermes' own memory, and an evidence-status table that distinguishes an executor reporting completion from a verified, gate-checked result.
summary.cons: As stated in the README, no measured benchmark run comparing Hermes alone against Hermes through OMH has been published yet, so the claimed cost and speed differences from that comparison are not yet backed by public results; alternative installers via Homebrew, Bun, and npm are noted as public only starting from v1.0.6.
summary.fit: Since OMH is presented as an addition that runs alongside Hermes Agent rather than replacing it, it appears intended for existing Hermes Agent users seeking a governed routing, coding-delegation, and memory layer rather than as a standalone alternative.

repos.name: localsend / localsend
repos.description: An open-source cross-platform alternative to AirDrop

summary.goal: LocalSend is documented as a free, open-source, cross-platform app that lets users securely share files and messages with nearby devices over a local network without needing an internet connection, using a REST API secured by HTTPS with certificates generated on the fly on each device.
summary.usage: It is recommended to install LocalSend from an app store or package manager. A terminal client is also documented: run `localsend-cli send report.pdf photo.jpg ./project-backup` to send files/directories, optionally adding `--to "Cute Tomato"` or `--to 192.168.27.26` to target a specific device by alias or IP address.
summary.pros: The README lists support for many platforms in one project (Windows, macOS, Linux, Android, iOS, Fire OS), operation without an internet connection or third-party servers, and signed Windows binaries.
summary.cons: The README notes the app has no auto-update, so users are advised to reinstall via an app store or package manager for updates; it also documents that firewall configuration (allowing TCP/UDP port 53317) may be required for sending and receiving to work correctly.
summary.fit: Based on the README, LocalSend appears best suited for offline, local-network file and message transfers between nearby devices, rather than transfers over the internet or to remote destinations.

repos.name: dani-garcia / vaultwarden
repos.description: Unofficial Bitwarden compatible server written in Rust, formerly known as bitwarden_rs

summary.goal: Vaultwarden is an alternative server implementation of the Bitwarden Client API, written in Rust, compatible with official Bitwarden clients, and intended for self-hosted deployment as a lighter alternative to the official, more resource-heavy service.
summary.usage: The recommended installation method is via container images published to ghcr.io, docker.io, and quay.io. A typical setup uses `docker pull vaultwarden/server:latest` followed by `docker run --detach --name vaultwarden --env DOMAIN="https://vw.domain.tld" --volume /vw-data/:/data/ --restart unless-stopped --publish 127.0.0.1:8000:80 vaultwarden/server:latest`.
summary.pros: The README documents a nearly complete implementation of the Bitwarden Client API, including personal vaults, Send, attachments, organizations, multi-factor authentication, emergency access, and an admin backend, alongside active community channels (Matrix, GitHub Discussions, Discourse).
summary.cons: The documentation states HTTPS and a secure context are required for the web-vault's Web Crypto API to function, so a reverse proxy or other HTTPS setup appears to be a prerequisite for full usability, which may add operational complexity for self-hosters.
summary.fit: Maintainers describe the project as focused on serving the self-hosting community, including individuals, families, and small organizations, though it is explicitly not associated with Bitwarden, Inc., cautiously suggesting it best suits users comfortable managing their own infrastructure and backups.

repos.name: TauricResearch / TradingAgents
repos.description: TradingAgents: Multi-Agents LLM Financial Trading Framework

summary.goal: TradingAgents is a multi-agent LLM-based financial trading framework built with LangGraph. It coordinates specialized agents — fundamentals, sentiment, news, and technical analysts, bullish/bearish researchers, a trader, and a risk-management/portfolio-manager team — to evaluate market conditions and produce trading decisions. The README states the framework is designed for research purposes and is not intended as financial, investment, or trading advice.
summary.usage: Install by cloning the repository (`git clone https://github.com/TauricResearch/TradingAgents.git`) and running `pip install .` inside it, optionally in a Python 3.12 virtual environment. Launch the interactive CLI with `tradingagents` (or `python -m cli.main`) to pick tickers, analysis date, LLM provider, and research depth. It can also be used directly in Python via the `TradingAgentsGraph` class and its `.propagate()` method, or run via Docker.
summary.pros: The framework supports numerous LLM providers (OpenAI, Google, Anthropic, xAI, DeepSeek, Qwen, GLM, MiniMax, OpenRouter, Ollama, Azure), works across multiple markets and asset types using Yahoo Finance tickers, and persists a decision log across runs plus offers opt-in checkpoint resume — features that appear to add resilience for longer or repeated analyses.
summary.cons: Because output is LLM-driven, two runs on the same ticker and date can differ due to non-deterministic model sampling and live news/social data changing over time; the current curated models are described as reasoning-first and largely ignoring temperature settings, so tighter reproducibility likely requires explicitly selecting a non-reasoning model.
summary.fit: The README frames this as a research scaffold for studying multi-agent market analysis rather than a strategy with a fixed, replicable return, suggesting it is best suited to research and experimentation contexts rather than production trading decisions.

repos.name: ruvnet / RuView
repos.description: π RuView turns commodity WiFi signals into real-time spatial intelligence, vital sign monitoring, and presence detection — all without a single pixel of video.

summary.goal: RuView is presented as a WiFi sensing platform that converts ordinary WiFi radio signals into spatial intelligence. It uses Channel State Information (CSI) captured by ESP32 sensors to detect presence, breathing rate, heart rate, activity, and body pose without cameras or wearables.
summary.usage: Documented setup options include Python packages via `pip install ruview` (or alias `wifi-densepose`), a Docker image (`docker pull ruvnet/wifi-densepose:latest`) for simulated-data evaluation, and a companion CLI invoked with `npx @ruvnet/ruview@0.4.0 doctor`. The platform is described as integrating with Home Assistant via MQTT, and with Apple Home, Google Home, and Alexa through the same bridge or a Matter endpoint.
summary.pros: The README lists an MIT license, a Rust 1.85+ toolchain, 1463 passing tests, and multi-architecture Docker support (amd64/arm64) as project attributes. It also cites low per-zone hardware costs (roughly $0-$9), no camera requirement, ability to sense through walls and in darkness, and use of already-deployed WiFi infrastructure.
summary.cons: The project is labeled 'Beta software' under active development, with documented limitations: ESP32-C3 and original ESP32 boards are unsupported, single-node deployments have limited spatial resolution, and camera-free pose accuracy is currently low (PCK@20 ≈ 2.5%), with further data-collection and evaluation phases still pending.
summary.fit: The README states these are research and prototype applications, not medical devices, emergency systems, or safety-certified controls, and that CSI-capable hardware such as ESP32-S3 is recommended for full sensing capability; this suggests the platform may suit hobbyist and research use more than production safety-critical deployments, though this framing is a cautious inference rather than an explicit README claim.

repos.name: tech-leads-club / agent-skills
repos.description: The secure, validated skill registry for professional AI coding agents. Extend Antigravity, Claude Code, Cursor, Copilot and more with absolute confidence.

summary.goal: Agent Skills is an npm-distributed registry of curated, security-reviewed skills — packaged instructions and resources — that extend AI coding agents such as Claude Code, Cursor, and others with new workflows and specialized knowledge.
summary.usage: Skills are installed by running `npx @tech-leads-club/agent-skills`, which launches an interactive wizard for choosing skills, target agents, install method (copy or symlink), and scope. Direct CLI commands are also available, e.g. `agent-skills install -s tlc-spec-driven`, alongside list, update, remove, cache, and audit subcommands; skills can also be served to MCP-compatible clients via the `@tech-leads-club/agent-skills-mcp` server.
summary.pros: Every skill is scanned with Snyk Agent Scan before publishing, the CLI applies defense-in-depth measures (sanitization, path isolation, symlink guards, atomic lockfile, audit trail), the codebase is stated to be 100% open source with CI static analysis, and it supports a wide range of Tier 1-3 agents including Claude Code, Cursor, and GitHub Copilot.
summary.cons: Node.js >=22 is required, and using the skills catalog requires mandatory attribution to Tech Leads Club regardless of context; third-party skills retain separate licenses that need individual checking.
summary.fit: Given its broad multi-agent support and stated security tooling, it may suit teams or developers already using agents like Claude Code or Cursor who want a centrally managed, vetted source of reusable skills rather than an open marketplace.

repos.name: OpenBMB / VoxCPM
repos.description: VoxCPM2: Tokenizer-Free TTS for Multilingual Speech Generation, Creative Voice Design, and True-to-Life Cloning

summary.goal: VoxCPM2 is a tokenizer-free, diffusion autoregressive Text-to-Speech (TTS) system from OpenBMB. It is a 2B-parameter model trained on over 2 million hours of multilingual speech data, supporting 30 languages, natural-language Voice Design, Controllable Voice Cloning, and 48kHz studio-quality audio output.
summary.usage: Install with `pip install voxcpm`, then load the model in Python via `VoxCPM.from_pretrained("openbmb/VoxCPM2", load_denoiser=False)` and call `model.generate(text=...)` to synthesize speech, saving output with `soundfile`. A CLI (`voxcpm design`, `voxcpm clone`) and a web demo (`python app.py`) are also documented.
summary.pros: Highlighted capabilities include 30-language synthesis without language tags, voice design from text descriptions with no reference audio, controllable cloning with style guidance, and real-time streaming with reported RTF as low as ~0.3 on an RTX 4090 (~0.13 with accelerated serving). Weights and code are released under the Apache-2.0 license for commercial use.
summary.cons: Requirements include Python ≥3.10 (<3.13), PyTorch ≥2.5.0, and CUDA ≥12.0, which may limit compatibility with older environments. The README also notes that Voice Design and Controllable Voice Cloning results can vary between runs, sometimes requiring 1-3 generation attempts to obtain the desired output.
summary.fit: The project appears suited for multilingual speech synthesis, voice cloning, and voice design applications, with documented production deployment paths via Nano-vLLM, vLLM-Omni, or llama.cpp-omni for GPU or on-device serving, and supports SFT/LoRA fine-tuning with as little as 5-10 minutes of audio.

repos.name: huggingface / transformers
repos.description: 🤗 Transformers: the model-definition framework for state-of-the-art machine learning models in text, vision, audio, and multimodal models, for both inference and training.

summary.goal: Transformers acts as a model-definition framework for state-of-the-art machine learning across text, vision, audio, video, and multimodal tasks, supporting both inference and training, and centralizing model definitions so they work across the broader ecosystem of training and inference frameworks.
summary.usage: After installing Python 3.10+ and PyTorch 2.5+, install the library with `pip install "transformers[torch]"`. Use the high-level `Pipeline` API (e.g. `pipeline(task="text-generation", model="Qwen/Qwen2.5-1.5B")`) for inference, or chat with a model from the command line via `transformers chat Qwen/Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct`.
summary.pros: It offers a unified API with only three main classes to learn, access to over 1M+ pretrained checkpoints on the Hugging Face Hub, and compatibility with numerous training frameworks (Axolotl, DeepSpeed, FSDP) and inference engines (vLLM, SGLang, TGI).
summary.cons: The README notes Transformers is not a modular toolbox of reusable building blocks—model files intentionally avoid extra abstractions—and its training API is optimized specifically for PyTorch models, so generic training loops may require a separate library such as Accelerate.
summary.fit: This makes it a good fit for developers and researchers who want ready-to-use, state-of-the-art models across modalities, but it may be less suited for teams needing a fully customizable neural-network building-block toolbox or generic (non-PyTorch-centric) training loops, and included example scripts may need adaptation to specific use cases.

repos.name: Crosstalk-Solutions / project-nomad
repos.description: Project NOMAD is an offline-first knowledge and education server. Wikipedia, thousands of books, courses, maps, and optional local AI, all running on hardware you own with no internet required.

summary.goal: Project NOMAD is described as a self-contained, offline-first knowledge and education server that bundles tools, reference content, and AI features to keep users informed without requiring an internet connection.
summary.usage: It installs on Debian-based systems (Ubuntu 26.04 LTS recommended, with 24.04 LTS and Debian 12 also supported) via a terminal-based quick-install script ending in `sudo bash install_nomad.sh`, run with sudo/root privileges. Afterward, the Command Center is reached in a browser at `http://localhost:8080`. An advanced route using `docker compose up -d` is also documented for users who prefer manual Docker configuration.

The README also notes AI tools are best run on GPU-backed hardware, suggesting full AI functionality may be constrained on lightweight, minimum-spec systems.
summary.fit: Given its terminal-based, sudo-driven, Docker-oriented installation on Debian-based OSes, NOMAD seems best suited to users comfortable with Linux command-line setup and container concepts seeking an offline reference and AI toolkit, rather than a plug-and-play appliance for non-technical users.

repos.name: reconurge / flowsint
repos.description: A modern platform for visual, flexible, and extensible graph-based investigations. For cybersecurity analysts and investigators.

The app becomes accessible at http://localhost:5173/register to create an account.
summary.pros: The README lists a wide range of enrichers spanning domain, IP, ASN, CIDR, social media, organization, cryptocurrency, website, email, phone, and individual categories. It also states the frontend is built for performance, with no lag even on thousands of nodes, and that data is stored on the user's machine for privacy.

Before exposing an installation to a network, users must manually change default secrets such as AUTH_SECRET and MASTER_VAULT_KEY_V1 in .env, suggesting default configurations may not be safe for network deployment without modification.
summary.fit: According to the README, Flowsint was created to assist cybersecurity researchers and analysts, journalists and OSINT investigators, law enforcement or fraud investigation teams, and organizations conducting internal threat intelligence. It explicitly states the tool must not be used for unauthorized intrusion, surveillance, harassment, doxxing, or privacy law violations.

repos.name: peetzweg / opendisplay
repos.description: Free, open-source Sidecar/Duet alternative — use your iPhone or iPad as a true second monitor for your Mac over USB or WiFi. Low latency H.264, Retina HiDPI, touch input.

summary.goal: OpenDisplay turns spare iPhones, iPads, or Macs into second monitors for a Mac, positioned as a free, open-source, self-hosted alternative to Apple Sidecar, Duet Display, and Luna Display, providing true extended-display support rather than mirroring.
summary.usage: Users install a Mac sender app and an iOS (or OpenDisplay Receiver) app. Prebuilt DMGs come from the latest release at https://github.com/peetzweg/opendisplay/releases/latest, and the iOS app can be joined via TestFlight at https://testflight.apple.com/join/3NYaY11c. Building from source uses `brew install xcodegen`, `git clone https://github.com/peetzweg/opendisplay.git`, then `./generate.sh` and `./run.sh`; connections run over USB or WiFi via Bonjour, with the receiver on port 9000.
summary.pros: Documented features include true display extension (not just mirroring), USB-wired low-latency streaming with no extra network tools, zero-config WiFi discovery, Retina/HiDPI pixel matching, built-in touch and scroll input, and self-hosted operation with no servers or accounts.
summary.cons: Because the virtual-display feature relies on the private CGVirtualDisplay API, the README notes it could break on a macOS update, a risk it says applies to comparable virtual-display products; WiFi mode also requires Local Network permission on both devices, which can fail silently if not granted.
summary.fit: It appears suited to Mac users with a spare iPhone, iPad, or older Mac who want an extended display without a subscription or dongle; the Receiver app needs macOS 12 or newer, the sending Mac needs macOS 14, and compatible receiver devices run iOS 16.4+.

repos.name: SnailSploit / Claude-Red

summary.cons: Roadmap phases 1, 2, 4, 5, and 6 are still listed as 'Planned,' so some announced coverage (e.g., cloud identity, additional web fundamentals) appears not yet implemented despite a stated target of roughly 130 skills. Effective use likely also depends on familiarity with the Claude Skills system's SKILL.md conventions.
summary.fit: This project appears best suited to security practitioners already working within the Claude Skills ecosystem or Claude Code who need structured, on-demand offensive methodology for authorized testing, research, or CTF contexts.

repos.name: ayghri / i-have-adhd

summary.pros: The skill enforces 10 documented rules, including leading with the next action, numbering multi-step tasks, ending with one concrete next step, suppressing tangents, and capping lists to 5 items; the README illustrates this with a before/after example contrasting a verbose response with a terse, actionable one.

The README also notes the approach is adapted for how an LLM should respond, not for how a person should organize their day, suggesting it may not function as a general ADHD management tool despite its name.

repos.name: bilawalsidhu / gods-eye-view

repos.name: affaan-m / ECC

summary.fit: ECC appears best suited for teams already standardized on Claude Code who want a structured, tool-assisted development workflow with reusable skills and security scanning. repos.name: openai / plugins

repos.name: DietrichGebert / ponytail
repos.description: Makes your AI agent think like the laziest senior dev in the room. The best code is the code you never wrote.

repos.name: mksglu / context-mode
repos.description: Context window optimization for AI coding agents. Sandboxes tool output (98% reduction), persists session memory, and   enforces routing across 17 platforms via MCP + hooks.

summary.goal: Context Mode is an MCP (Model Context Protocol) server built for AI coding agents. summary.usage: Claude Code users install it as a plugin with `/plugin marketplace add mksglu/context-mode` followed by `/plugin install context-mode@context-mode`, then restart Claude Code and run the diagnostics command to confirm the install. The documented prerequisite for this plugin path is Claude Code v1.0.33+; other supported clients register the same server as an MCP tool provider instead.
summary.pros: The README states that raw command output is processed inside an isolated sandbox subprocess, so only relevant results reach the conversation, with one documented example of a 315 KB session output reduced to about 5.4 KB — roughly a 98% reduction. It also documents no telemetry and no required account, since session data stays local.
summary.cons: On platforms without hook support, such as the Antigravity IDE and Zed, the README states that routing enforcement depends on a manually copied instruction file rather than automatic interception, and estimates this reaches only about 60% of the context savings achieved with hooks. The Cursor plugin is also documented as still awaiting marketplace review.
summary.fit: Based on the company logos presented as users, Context Mode appears suited to both individual developers and engineering teams working across MCP-compatible AI coding clients — the README documents support for 17 such clients plus an OpenClaw gateway integration. It is released under the Elastic License 2.0, a source-available license disallowing hosted or managed-service offerings.

repos.name: heygen-com / hyperframes

repos.name: tt-a1i / archify

repos.name: microsoft / markitdown

repos.name: blader / humanizer

repos.name: max-sixty / worktrunk

repos.name: coreyhaines31 / marketingskills

summary.pros: The library bundles skills spanning CAD generation with STEP/STL/3MF/GLB export, a step.parts finder for off-the-shelf parts, DXF drawing creation, URDF/SRDF/SDF robot-description authoring, G-code slicing, and Bambu Labs print handling, released under the MIT license.
summary.cons: Running `npx skills update` only refreshes skills already present in the lockfile and silently misses skills added in newer releases, so keeping the full skill set current relies on rerunning `npx skills add` instead.
summary.fit: This appears best suited to agent-driven CAD/robotics workflows within supported agent environments such as Codex, Claude Code, and Grok Build, though not every supported agent is explicitly enumerated.

repos.name: petergyang / no-ai-slop
repos.description: Removes 20+ patterns of AI slop from any piece of writing.

summary.goal: No AI Slop is a skill for removing more than 20 documented patterns of "AI slop" writing—such as binary contrasts ("It's not X. It's Y."), throat-clearing openers, and fake-profound endings—while aiming to preserve the writer's personal voice.
summary.usage: Install it by pasting "Install the /no-ai-slop skill globally from https://github.com/petergyang/no-ai-slop" into ChatGPT, Claude Code, Codex, or another coding agent, or by running npx skills add petergyang/no-ai-slop --skill no-ai-slop --global --yes. Then invoke /no-ai-slop (your writing) to edit text, or /no-ai-slop is this slop? (your writing) to detect slop patterns.
summary.pros: The README states the editing mode preserves personal voice and lists what it changed, while the detection mode quotes every slop pattern found. It also checks writing fundamentals such as leading with the point, active voice, and concrete detail over abstraction.
summary.cons: The detection mode explicitly quotes slop patterns "without guessing whether AI wrote the text," so it likely cannot confirm authorship, only flag matching phrasing patterns.
summary.fit: Given its install path, it appears best suited to people already working inside ChatGPT, Claude Code, Codex, or similar coding-agent environments to review or generate writing.

repos.name: github / spec-kit
repos.description: 💫 Toolkit to help you get started with Spec-Driven Development

summary.goal: Spec Kit is an open source toolkit for Spec-Driven Development (SDD), a workflow where specifications are written and refined before implementation and then used to generate working code with any AI coding agent.
summary.usage: Install with `uv tool install specify-cli --from git+https://github.com/github/spec-kit.git@vX.Y.Z`, then run `specify init my-project --integration copilot` and `cd my-project` to scaffold a project. From there, agents run slash commands such as /speckit.constitution, /speckit.specify, /speckit.plan, /speckit.tasks, and /speckit.implement to move from principles to a completed feature.
summary.pros: Spec Kit bundles two optional, opt-in workflows beyond the core SDD flow: bug fixing (assess → fix → test) and idea assessment (intake → research → define → shape → decide). It also integrates with 30+ AI coding agents, both CLI tools and IDE-based assistants.
summary.cons: Using Spec Kit requires several prerequisites: uv (or pipx for persistent installs), Python 3.11+, Git, and a supported AI coding agent, so setup is not a single self-contained step. Community-created extensions, presets, and bundles are maintained independently of the core project.
summary.fit: Given its structured, multi-phase workflow spanning greenfield development, creative exploration, and iterative/brownfield enhancement, Spec Kit appears best suited to teams and organizations that already use AI coding agents and want a repeatable, documented process for translating specifications into implementations.

repos.name: kunchenguid / firstmate
repos.description: Talk to one agent. Ship with a crew.

summary.goal: firstmate is documented as an agent distro—not a model, harness, skill, MCP server, or CLI—that lets a single primary agent (the 'first mate') dispatch tasks to a crew of autonomous coding agents ('crewmates'), each working in an isolated git worktree, producing pull requests, approved local merges, or investigation reports.
summary.usage: Setup requires git, the GitHub CLI authenticated via `gh auth login`, and a supported harness such as Claude Code, Grok, or Pi. Installation is `git clone https://github.com/kunchenguid/firstmate` followed by `cd firstmate`, then launching a harness like `claude`, after which AGENTS.md guides the session.
summary.pros: Documented benefits include a single point of contact (the first mate) instead of juggling multiple terminals, a visible crew running in tmux windows or other backend tabs, disposable per-task git worktrees via treehouse, event-driven zero-token supervision, and restart-proof state that persists on disk.
summary.cons: Running a primary session depends on a verified harness with its own setup, such as Grok needing `--trust` once per clone or Cursor Agent CLI needing `--trust` and lacking a turn-end hook in headless mode. The Codex App backend is explicitly documented as not yet a supported runtime backend.
summary.fit: Based on its described features, firstmate appears best suited to developers on macOS or Linux who want to run multiple coding tasks in parallel across a GitHub repository, though its practical value likely depends on which harness and backend they already use.

repos.name: omacom / omarchy
repos.description: Beautiful, Modern & Opinionated Linux

summary.goal: Omarchy is presented as a Linux distribution created by DHH, described as "beautiful, fun & agentic," with more information available at https://omarchy.org.
summary.usage: Its documentation is organized in a manual/ directory, also mirrored at https://learn.omacom.io/2/the-omarchy-manual, covering topics such as Getting Started, Hotkeys, and the Omarchy CLI; since no separate installation command is given, setup and navigation appear to begin with the "Getting Started" and "Coming From Mac or Windows" manual pages.
summary.pros: It is released under the MIT License (https://opensource.org/licenses/MIT), and its manual spans roughly fifty pages covering applications, configuration, theming, hardware, security, and troubleshooting topics.
summary.cons: Because documentation is split across dozens of separate manual files rather than one consolidated guide, users may need to check multiple pages to piece together full setup or configuration details, and cross-platform users may need to rely on the separate "Windows VM" and "Mac support" pages, suggesting native support is Linux-centric.
summary.fit: Omarchy appears best suited to Linux users wanting a preconfigured desktop environment with built-in AI, development, and theming tools, though platform or hardware prerequisites beyond the listed manual topics are not specified.

repos.name: anthropics / claude-plugins-community
repos.description: Community plugin marketplace for Claude Cowork and Claude Code. Read-only mirror — submit plugins at clau.de/plugin-directory-submission.

summary.goal: Claude Plugins — Community is documented as a read-only mirror of the community plugin marketplace for Claude Cowork and Claude Code. The .claude-plugin/marketplace.json file lists plugins available for installation, synced nightly from Anthropic's internal review pipeline.
summary.usage: Plugins can be installed from claude.com/plugins/ for Claude Cowork, or through the Claude Code CLI, which requires first adding the marketplace and then installing a specific plugin by running `claude plugin marketplace add anthropics/claude-plugins-community` followed by `claude plugin install <plugin-name>@claude-community`.
summary.pros: Every listed plugin has passed automated security scanning and been approved for distribution before appearing in the marketplace. Submissions go through a single, centralized intake point at clau.de/plugin-directory-submission rather than ad hoc channels.
summary.cons: Because the marketplace list syncs only nightly from an internal pipeline, the visible plugin set may lag behind the actual review state by up to a day; exact update timing and discrepancy handling are not detailed in the source material.
summary.fit: This repository appears suited for users who want to browse and install pre-vetted plugins through the documented web interface or CLI, rather than contribute code directly, since pull requests opened against the repo are closed automatically.

repos.name: AprilNEA / OpenLogi
repos.description: ⚡️A native, local-first alternative to Logitech Options+, written in Rust 🦀 — remap buttons, DPI, and SmartShift over HID++. No account, no telemetry.

summary.goal: OpenLogi is a native, local-first alternative to Logitech Options+, written in Rust, that unlocks additional capabilities of Logitech mice, keyboards, and webcams over the HID++ and UVC protocols. It runs on macOS, Linux, and Windows and is currently under active development, so features and configuration may still change.
summary.usage: Before installing, quit Logi Options+, since the two applications cannot share HID++ access to the same receiver. On macOS 13 or later, install via Homebrew with `brew install --cask openlogi`. Linux users can instead install a `.deb` package from the latest GitHub release (https://github.com/AprilNEA/OpenLogi/releases/latest) using `sudo dpkg -i openlogi-*.deb`.
summary.pros: OpenLogi keeps a light native Rust/GPUI footprint, treats Linux as a first-class platform, and stores all settings in one syncable TOML file. It supports assigning gesture roles to any physical button, per-application profile overlays, and a scriptable CLI alongside the GUI. Device-specific controls include DPI presets, SmartShift wheel settings, keyboard RGB lighting, and detailed UVC webcam image adjustments.
summary.cons: The project is explicitly marked as under active development and not yet stable, meaning features and configuration format may change before a stable release. Pre-built Linux packages require GLIBC 2.35 or newer (an Ubuntu 22.04 baseline), which could limit compatibility with older Linux distributions.
summary.fit: OpenLogi may suit users who want a native, open-source, cross-platform replacement for Logitech Options+ with scriptable configuration, particularly on Linux where Options+ has no official client. It is not affiliated with Logitech, so it could be less suitable for users who need official vendor support or a fully stabilized release.

repos.name: cursor / plugins
repos.description: Cursor plugin specification and official plugins

summary.goal: This repository hosts official Cursor plugins for popular developer tools, frameworks, and SaaS products. Each plugin lives in its own standalone directory at the repository root, defined by a `.cursor-plugin/plugin.json` manifest, and covers categories such as Developer Tools, Productivity, and Integrations.
summary.usage: The repository follows a multi-plugin marketplace layout: the root `.cursor-plugin/marketplace.json` file lists all plugins, while each plugin directory contains its own `.cursor-plugin/plugin.json` manifest along with optional `skills/`, `rules/`, and `mcp.json` files, plus its own README, CHANGELOG, and LICENSE.
summary.pros: The collection spans dozens of plugins, including developer-focused tools like GitHub, Playwright, and Cursor SDK, alongside productivity and SaaS integrations such as Gmail, Google Calendar, Salesforce, and HubSpot, offering broad coverage across coding, collaboration, and business workflows.
summary.cons: Because each plugin targets a distinct third-party service or tool with its own manifest and likely its own authentication requirements, adopting multiple plugins may involve separate per-service setup; the README does not detail these individual configuration steps.
summary.fit: This repository appears best suited for teams and developers already using the Cursor platform who want to extend it with additional developer-tool or SaaS integrations, rather than as a standalone application.

repos.name: volcengine / OpenViking
repos.description: Self-evolving Context Database for AI Agents. Unify Agent Memory, Knowledge RAG and Skills.

summary.goal: OpenViking is presented as an open-source context database for AI agents, giving them a place to store knowledge, remember users, and reuse experience across sessions. It organizes this context as a virtual filesystem reachable through a viking:// URI scheme, browsable with commands such as ls, tree, read, and write.
summary.usage: Installation starts with `pip install openviking --upgrade`, then `openviking-server init` configures provider and model settings before the server is started. Users then rely on the bundled `ov` CLI to import and search resources, for example adding a GitHub repository and running semantic queries against it. It requires Python 3.10+ and access to an embedding model plus a VLM, cloud-hosted or local.
summary.pros: According to the project's benchmark report, an OpenViking 0.3.22 evaluation found three agent integrations rising from 24–57% to 80–83% accuracy on the LoCoMo memory benchmark, while input tokens dropped 34.3–91.0% and query latency dropped 58.45–66.10%. On tau2-bench, task success rose by +6.87pp (retail) and +11.87pp (airline) versus the same LLM without memory. These figures come from the specific models and setups tested and may not generalize to every configuration.
summary.cons: Running OpenViking requires Python 3.10+ plus access to both an embedding model and a VLM, cloud-hosted or local, before the server will start. The core project is released under AGPLv3, and documentation advises configuring authentication before exposing a deployed server beyond localhost.
summary.fit: The open-source server can be self-hosted under AGPLv3 with no activation key, suiting teams building agent integrations that need persistent, cross-session memory. Organizations wanting managed hosting or distributed production deployments can instead choose the Managed SaaS or license-key-based Self-Managed (BYOC) commercial editions; the companion desktop console remains in beta for macOS and Windows x64.

repos.name: freestylefly / awesome-gpt-image-2
repos.description: Prompt as Code | GPT Image 2 / 2.5 提示词与案例库，530+ 个案例、20+ 套工业级模板与可复用 Skills，新增 2.5 同提示词对比专区，附完整提示词与生成记录，持续更新。

It documents 544 reverse-engineered cases plus reusable templates, aiming to turn prose-style prompts into structured, composable protocols for batch and automation-friendly image generation, including a GPT Image 2.5 spotlight section.
summary.usage: Users can browse the case gallery and templates directly on GitHub, or explore the companion site at https://gpt-image2.canghe.ai. To add the bundled Agent Skill, run `npx skills add freestylefly/awesome-gpt-image-2 --skill gpt-image-2-style-library --agent claude-code codex --global --yes --copy`, or inside Claude Code run `/plugin marketplace add freestylefly/awesome-gpt-image-2`.
summary.pros: The repository organizes 544 cases into clear categories (UI, posters, branding, photography, and more) alongside matching prompt templates, and ships an installable Agent Skill compatible with Claude Code, Codex, and Cursor, plus a visual website for side-by-side prompt comparison.
summary.cons: Enabling the companion website's paid generation and billing features requires configuring numerous Vercel environment variables (Supabase, Stripe, Google Analytics) and applying multiple Supabase SQL migrations in sequence, an operational setup that goes beyond simply browsing the static prompt library.
summary.fit: The structured, template-based approach seems best suited to users building repeatable or automated image-generation workflows with agent tools rather than one-off casual prompting, though effectiveness depends on access to the underlying GPT-Image2 model.

repos.name: modular / modular
repos.description: The Modular Platform (includes MAX & Mojo)

summary.goal: This repository hosts open-source components of the Modular Platform, described as a unified platform for AI development and deployment. It includes the MAX Framework and the Mojo Language, covering the compiler, standard library, accelerator library, inference server, and model pipelines documented in the repo.
summary.usage: Getting started with the MAX framework involves the quickstart guide at https://max.modular.com/get-started, used for serving a model. Getting started with Mojo involves the quickstart guide at https://mojolang.org/docs/manual/quickstart/. Contributions to the Mojo standard library, MAX accelerator library, or MAX model architectures should begin by reading CONTRIBUTING.md.
summary.pros: The repo lists distinct components: the Mojo compiler, Mojo standard library, MAX accelerator library, an MAX inference server with an OpenAI-compatible endpoint, Python-based MAX model pipelines, and code examples. It accepts community contributions to the standard library, accelerator library, model architectures, and documentation.

MAX usage and distribution follow a separate Modular Community License apart from the repository's Apache License v2.0 license, which could mean users need to review third-party library licenses themselves.

repos.name: akitaonrails / ai-memory
repos.description: Solution for long term memory for agent coding CLIs and to facilitate handoff between different agent vendors

summary.goal: ai-memory is described as long-term memory for AI coding agents, letting a session started in Claude Code continue in another agent such as OpenAI Codex in the same directory without re-explaining the architecture, failed approaches, or open questions.
summary.usage: Quick start uses Docker: run `docker run -d --name ai-memory --restart unless-stopped -p 127.0.0.1:49374:49374 -v ai-memory-data:/data docker.io/akitaonrails/ai-memory:latest` to start the server, then `ai-memory install-mcp --client claude-code --apply` and `ai-memory install-hooks --agent claude-code --apply` to wire in an agent CLI.
summary.pros: According to the documentation, its source of truth is plain markdown files in a git-backed wiki, and the default path is said to use zero LLM calls, so capture, search, and handoffs reportedly work without any API key.
summary.cons: The documented quick-start default runs with no authentication and binds only to loopback, so exposing the server on a LAN reportedly requires adding a bearer token as an extra step; native Windows support is listed as experimental rather than fully supported.
summary.fit: The project appears suited to both a single-user workstation and teams running a shared server, and setup requires Docker/Podman or, on Arch Linux, AUR packages.

summary.goal: vphone-cli boots a virtual iPhone using Apple's Virtualization.framework, built on PCC research VM infrastructure. It targets Apple Silicon Macs running macOS 15+ (Sequoia).
summary.usage: Install via Homebrew with `brew install zqxwce/tap/vphone-cli`, or build from source by cloning the repo (`git clone --recurse-submodules https://github.com/Lakr233/vphone-cli.git`) and running the provided setup and build scripts. A virtual iPhone can then be created and started with `vphone-cli vm create myphone -V jb` followed by `vphone-cli vm launch myphone`, which downloads firmware, patches the boot chain, performs a DFU restore, and installs the chosen CFW variant.
summary.pros: The `vm create` command automates the entire pipeline from download to first boot in a single step. Five firmware variants (`less` through `exp`) offer graduated levels of security bypass, from mitigation-preserving to full jailbreak with anti-VM-detection patches. A host control socket enables programmatic screenshots, touch, and input for automated or AI-driven testing.
summary.cons: Setup requires relaxing macOS SIP and AMFI protections on the host to allow unsigned binaries with private entitlements, a change that likely reduces the host's overall security posture. The documentation also notes a known bug in the `ldid-procursus` tool (up to version 2.1.5-procursus7) that can cause the `cfw install` step to hang with unbounded memory growth, requiring a rebuild from source as a workaround.
summary.fit: The tool appears suited to developers and security researchers who need an isolated virtual iPhone environment on Apple Silicon for jailbreak research, firmware patch testing, or automated/AI-driven app testing. It is not intended for use inside a nested virtual machine host, since virtualization-based guest boot cannot nest on such configurations.

repos.name: apache / maka
repos.description: Apache Maka (Incubating) is a high-performance agent workspace that keeps a complete record of everything it did.

summary.goal: Apache Maka (Incubating) is presented as a high-performance agent workspace that keeps a complete, append-only record of everything it does, via a RuntimeEvent log capturing model messages, tool calls, and permission decisions. The README states results are benchmarked against other harnesses on the same model with an official verifier, with per-task results published in `docs/eval/`.
summary.usage: To build from source: `git clone https://github.com/apache/maka.git`, then `npm ci` and `npm run dev` to start the Desktop dev environment with HMR. Stated requirements are Node.js 22.19+ (CI uses Node.js 24), npm 11, Git, and ripgrep; Direct Peer/Peer Mesh development additionally needs Rust stable 1.98+.
summary.pros: According to the README, the RuntimeEvent log is the authoritative runtime record rather than just the UI or next prompt, sessions/settings/run records stay local while users supply their own model (cloud API, local model, or gateway), and Desktop, TUI/CLI, and Eval share a single Runtime Host execution authority.
summary.cons: The README notes Apache Maka has not made an official Apache release yet, so no signed source archive currently exists as the release artifact. It also states the project is under ASF incubation and active development, so data formats, CLI commands, and experimental capabilities may still change.
summary.fit: Based on the stated Desktop Nightly platform support (signed macOS Apple Silicon/Intel builds; unsigned Windows x64 and Linux x64/arm64 previews) and the explicit note that Nightly builds are not intended for production use, this suggests best fit for developers and testers building or evaluating agent harnesses locally.

repos.name: microsoft / data-formulator
repos.description: 🪄 Data Formulator is an interactive AI-powered data analysis system makes it easy to connect, explore and visualize data.

summary.goal: Data Formulator is a Microsoft Research project for AI-powered data visualization, combining UI interactions with natural language so analysts can explore data, branch into alternative analyses, and share results, starting from formats such as screenshots, text, CSV, or databases.
summary.usage: It can be installed and run locally via `uvx data_formulator` or `pip install data_formulator` followed by `python -m data_formulator`, which opens automatically at http://localhost:5567; a Docker option (`docker compose up --build`) is also documented, and unsigned preview desktop builds for Windows and macOS are available from CI artifacts.
summary.pros: The tool provides data connectors for multiple sources with a shared data memory, and 'Data Threads' that let users branch into different questions and compare paths without losing context. Charts are powered by the open-source Flint visualization language, and model support reportedly includes OpenAI, Azure, Ollama, and Anthropic via LiteLLM.
summary.cons: The downloadable desktop builds are described as automated preview builds that are not code-signed or notarized, so users must manually bypass Windows SmartScreen or macOS Gatekeeper warnings, and are advised to only do so when the archive came directly from the repository's workflow artifacts or releases.
summary.fit: Given its reliance on Python packaging tools (uv or pip) or Docker, and its browser-based interface, Data Formulator appears best suited for individual analysts or teams comfortable with local Python environments or containerized setups rather than a fully managed hosted product.

repos.name: public-apis / public-apis
repos.description: A collective list of free APIs

summary.goal: The public-apis/public-apis repository curates and categorizes free, public HTTP APIs across dozens of domains (from Animals to Weather) so developers can discover suitable APIs for their own projects.
summary.usage: Developers browse the category Index and the corresponding tables, each listing an API's name, description, required Auth type, HTTPS support, and CORS support, to find and integrate a fitting API; issues and pull requests are tracked at https://github.com/public-apis/public-apis/issues for community contributions.
summary.pros: The list is manually curated by community members and APILayer contributors, spans an extensive range of domains, and each entry documents authentication method, HTTPS availability, and CORS support, making it easier to compare candidate APIs before use.
summary.cons: Many entries mark CORS support as 'Unknown', so that compatibility detail may not be documented for every listed API, and users likely need to verify pricing, rate limits, and current availability directly with each third-party provider.
summary.fit: This resource suits developers and hobbyists searching for a specific type of free or freemium API (e.g., geocoding, currency exchange) rather than users needing a single, ready-to-use SDK or endpoint themselves, since it is only an index, not an API.

repos.name: google-research / timesfm
repos.description: TimesFM (Time Series Foundation Model) is a pretrained time-series foundation model developed by Google Research for time-series forecasting.

summary.goal: TimesFM is a pretrained time-series foundation model developed by Google Research for time-series forecasting, described in an ICML 2024 paper (https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.10688). The latest version, TimesFM 3.0, adds native multivariate forecasting and support for past-only and past-and-future covariates.
summary.usage: Install with pip install timesfm[torch] (or pip install timesfm[mlx] for Apple silicon), or run git clone https://github.com/google-research/timesfm.git for a local install. The README shows Python examples using the google/timesfm-3.0-pytorch checkpoint via TimesFM3Evaluator and ModelConfig for univariate and multivariate forecasting.
summary.pros: TimesFM 3.0 is documented as ranking #1 on the fev-bench, TIME Benchmark, and GIFT-Eval time-series foundation model benchmarks, and supports flexible covariate-based forecasting without per-task tuning.
summary.cons: TimesFM 3.0 pretrained weights are distributed under a separate license, timesfm-non-commercial-license-v1.0, restricted to non-commercial, non-production use, so commercial or production use of the default weights is not permitted; source code and weights up to version 2.5 remain Apache-2.0.
summary.fit: This project appears suited to researchers and developers exploring time-series forecasting, including multivariate and covariate-based use cases, though commercial or production deployments would likely need to account for the non-commercial licensing of the TimesFM 3.0 weights, and the repository states it is not an officially supported Google product.
